specPoints.text: describe the structures of an insect-pollinated and a wind-pollinated flower and explain how each is adapted for pollination

primer.text: Flowers cannot walk, so pollination depends on couriers. This note contrasts the two courier systems on the syllabus: flowers that hire insects with colour, scent and nectar, and flowers that let the wind do the deliveries. For each you will see how every structural detail, from petal size to filament length, earns its keep as an adaptation.

lessons.title: Insect-Pollinated Flowers
lessons.opening: An insect-visited flower runs a reward scheme: bold petals plus scent and nectar pull visitors in, and sticky pollen plus a sticky stigma make every visit count as a delivery between flowers.
keyPoints: Insect-pollinated flowers are large and brightly coloured so insects can spot them.
Scent and nectar reward visitors and push them to brush past the stamens.
Anthers sit on stiff filaments inside the flower so they rub pollen onto insect bodies.
Sticky stigmas positioned inside the flower catch pollen off arriving insects.

low.restatement: Colour, scent and nectar bring insects in; sticky pollen and sticky stigmas get the grains swapped between visits.
low.analogy: A shop with a bright window display and free samples: the customer leaves carrying crumbs to the next branch.
low.examPointer: Link every feature to its job — colour attracts, nectar rewards, stiff anthers load pollen, sticky stigmas unload it.

medium.restatement: The petals, scents and sugary rewards exist only to move pollen; the male parts are positioned where a feeding insect must brush them, and the female surface is tacky enough to strip grains off the visitor.
medium.analogy: A Velcro handshake: one side (the anther) coats the courier, the other (the stigma) grips the cargo on arrival.
medium.examPointer: Examiners want feature-to-function pairs, so name the structure and its adaptation in the same sentence.

check.stem: Why are the petals of an insect-pollinated flower large and brightly coloured?

options.text: To attract insects that carry pollen between flowers
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: To shield the ovules from rain
options.explanation: Petals are not the rain cover; sepals guard the bud.

options.text: To make the pollen fly further
options.explanation: Petal colour cannot launch pollen; a courier does the carrying.

options.text: To reflect heat away from the ovary
options.explanation: Temperature control is not a petal job here.

check.stem: Which structure produces and releases the pollen grains?

options.text: The anther
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The stigma
options.explanation: The stigma receives pollen; it never makes it.

options.text: The filament
options.explanation: The filament is the stalk that holds the anther up.

options.text: The sepal
options.explanation: The sepal protects the unopened bud.

check.stem: What keeps the anthers positioned so visiting insects cannot avoid them?

options.text: Stiff filaments holding them inside the flower where bodies must brush past
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Long floppy stalks hanging outside the petals
options.explanation: Hanging outside is the wind-pollinated design, not the insect one.

options.text: A ring of muscle around the ovary
options.explanation: Muscles belong to animal bodies, not flower stalks.

options.text: Sticky nectar gluing the anthers shut
options.explanation: Nectar rewards visitors; it does not anchor anthers.

check.stem: Why is a sticky stigma an advantage for an insect-pollinated flower?

options.text: It catches pollen grains off the bodies of brushing insects
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It dissolves the pollen to feed the style
options.explanation: The stigma collects grains; digestion happens later, after tube growth.

options.text: It stops insects from landing twice
options.explanation: Repeat visits are harmless; catching grains is the point.

options.text: It glues petals shut at night
options.explanation: Petal closure is not a stigma role.

check.stem: A bee enters a flower for nectar and leaves dusted with grains. Which sequence describes what it achieved?

options.text: It collected pollen while feeding and can deposit it on the next flower's stigma
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: It fertilised the flower it fed on
options.explanation: Feeding alone does not complete fertilisation; delivery to another stigma is the pollination step.

options.text: It destroyed the anthers by feeding
options.explanation: Feeding on nectar does not strip the anthers.

options.text: It carried nectar instead of pollen
options.explanation: The cargo that matters is pollen on the body, not nectar.

check.stem: State the flower structure whose job is to receive pollen grains.
check.modelAnswer: The stigma is the sticky female surface that receives pollen grains.

check.stem: Name the two flower parts that produce scent and nectar rewards for insect visitors.
check.modelAnswer: Scent plus nectar exist to draw insect visitors in and reward them for arriving.

check.stem: Explain why an insect-pollinated flower wastes no effort on tiny, dull petals.
check.modelAnswer: Dull small petals would fail the flower's only recruitment tool, since insects find these flowers by sight, so large bright petals are what attract the couriers.

check.stem: A gardener breeds a variety with almost no scent. Predict the effect on insect visits and explain your answer.
check.modelAnswer: Visits should drop, since scent and nectar exist to draw insects in, so a scentless variety loses its main long-range signal.

lessons.title: Wind-Pollinated Flowers
lessons.opening: A wind-pollinated flower hires no couriers, so it drops every attractant and rebuilds its male and female surfaces as open platforms: long dangling anthers shed grains into moving air, and feathery stigmas sweep them back out of it.
keyPoints: Wind-pollinated petals stay small and dull, commonly green or brown.
No scent or nectar is made, because producing them would waste energy.
Anthers hang outside the flower on long filaments so wind can carry pollen away.
Feathery stigmas hang outside the flower to trap airborne grains.

low.restatement: No colour, no scent, no nectar; the anthers and stigmas simply hang outside where the air flows.
low.analogy: A stall that skips advertising and just throws flyers into the street wind, with a wide net to catch neighbours' flyers.
low.examPointer: The wind design is the inverse of the insect design — quote the hanging anthers and feathery stigmas as the pair of adaptations.

medium.restatement: Because random airflow is unreliable, the flower compensates with sheer exposure: anthers on long filaments launch grains beyond the petals, and feathery stigmas present a wide sticky net to whatever drifts past.
medium.analogy: Fishing without bait, using many hooks: wasteful per cast, effective across thousands of tries.
medium.examPointer: Say why the waste is acceptable: grains are cheap to make in bulk, so exposure beats attraction for these flowers.

check.stem: Why do wind-pollinated flowers make no scent or nectar?

options.text: Because no couriers need rewarding, so producing them would waste energy
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Because scent would poison the pollen
options.explanation: Scent does not chemically harm pollen.

options.text: Because wind destroys scent molecules
options.explanation: The wind scatters smells; it does not make them pointless.

options.text: Because nectar dries out the anthers
options.explanation: Nectar does not drain the anthers.

check.stem: Which feature lets a wind-pollinated flower shed its grains into the moving air most easily?

options.text: Anthers hanging outside the flower on long filaments
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Anthers locked deep inside the petals
options.explanation: Deep placement would shield grains from the airflow.

options.text: Sticky pollen clumped on stiff stalks
options.explanation: Stickiness suits insect carriage, not wind release.

options.text: A feathery stigma inside the ovary
options.explanation: The stigma is female and sits outside, not in the ovary.

check.stem: What is the job of a feathery stigma in a wind-pollinated flower?

options.text: To present a wide surface that catches airborne pollen grains
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: To produce nectar for insects
options.explanation: Feathery stigmas do not reward couriers.

options.text: To wrap the seeds after fertilisation
options.explanation: Fruit, not stigma, wraps seeds.

options.text: To push the pollen tube down the style
options.explanation: The tube grows by itself; the stigma just receives grains.

check.stem: A wind-pollinated flower's petals are small and often green or brown. What does this contrast with?

options.text: The large, brightly coloured petals of insect-pollinated flowers
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: The sticky stigmas of insect-pollinated flowers
options.explanation: The contrast asked for is petal colour and size.

options.text: The long filaments of insect-pollinated flowers
options.explanation: Filament length is an anther feature, not a petal one.

options.text: The nectar of wind-pollinated flowers
options.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers make no nectar at all.

check.stem: Wind pollination is a numbers game. Why can these flowers afford to release so many grains that never land on a stigma?

options.text: Pollen is cheap to produce in bulk, and exposure beats attraction when no courier is hired
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Every grain is guided to a stigma by scent
options.explanation: Scent is absent in wind-pollinated flowers.

options.text: The wind carries each grain precisely
options.explanation: Airflow is random; most grains miss.

options.text: Grains that miss germinate on leaves
options.explanation: Missed grains are simply lost.

check.stem: State where the anthers of a wind-pollinated flower hang and why.
check.modelAnswer: The anthers hang outside the flower on long filaments so the wind can blow the pollen away.

check.stem: Describe the petals of a wind-pollinated flower.
check.modelAnswer: The petals keep a small, dull look, commonly green or brown.

check.stem: Explain why hanging both anthers and stigmas outside the flower suits wind pollination.
check.modelAnswer: Hanging outside puts the anthers directly in the airflow that carries grains away and puts the feathery stigmas in the path of grains drifting from other flowers.

check.stem: A grass flower growing in a sheltered, still courtyard sets few seeds. Suggest why, using the wind-pollination adaptation you have learned.
check.modelAnswer: With little moving air, the exposed anthers release pollen that never drifts far, so few grains reach the feathery stigmas of neighbouring flowers.

glossary.definition: The transfer of pollen from a male flower part to a female flower part of the same species.
The male flower structure that makes and releases pollen grains.
The female flower surface that receives pollen grains.
The structure inside the ovary that holds the female gamete of a plant.
